stories.head: Mexico captures FBI most-wanted cartel boss 'El Chapo Isidro'
stories.say: Mexican forces have captured Fausto Isidro Meza Flores, one of the FBI's ten most wanted, in a Friday night raid in Sinaloa that set off gun battles and burning roadblocks.
stories.stand: Special forces seized Fausto Isidro Meza Flores in Sinaloa, setting off clashes, road blockades and burning vehicles around the town of Guasave.
body: Mexican security forces captured Fausto Isidro Meza Flores, known as 'El Chapo Isidro', in a raid in Sinaloa state on Friday night, Mexico's National Defense Secretariat said on Saturday. He has been on the FBI's Ten Most Wanted list since February 2025.
Officials said troops were attacked with gunfire and explosives during the operation in Guasave. Meza Flores and two other leaders were flown to Mexico City on an air force plane.

Clashes, roadblocks and burning vehicles followed. Videos showed people fleeing gunfire at a baseball game in Guasave. The Mexican government said intelligence from the Trump administration helped but gave few details.

The FBI describes his group as a heavily armed drug-trafficking organisation. He was indicted in the US in 2012 and 2019, and the US had offered up to $5 million for information leading to his arrest.

stories.head: Russian cargo ship on fire in Gulf of Finland after drone strike
stories.say: A sanctioned Russian cargo ship bound for Kaliningrad caught fire in the Gulf of Finland on Saturday after two drones hit it, and its sixteen crew took to lifeboats.
stories.stand: Finland's armed forces said Ukraine was likely behind the attack on the Sparta II, which later drifted into Finnish waters.
body: Two drones struck a cargo ship bound for Russia's Kaliningrad exclave on Saturday morning, the governor of Russia's Leningrad region, Alexander Drozdenko, said. The ship was in international waters west of Gogland island in the eastern Gulf of Finland.

ABC News named the vessel as the Sparta II, which is under US sanctions. Its 16 crew escaped in lifeboats and were taken aboard another Russian ship. The burning vessel later drifted into Finnish waters.

A Finnish armed forces spokesperson said Ukraine was likely behind the attack. Finland's border guard said military cargo could not be ruled out. Finland imposed temporary air and sea restrictions, and Prime Minister Petteri Orpo said the war was spilling into the region.
No one has claimed the attack. Kaliningrad's governor said supplies to the exclave were not at risk.

stories.head: Iran says it fired missiles at US bases in Bahrain as tankers are hit
stories.say: Iranian media say Iran fired drones and ballistic missiles at four US bases in Bahrain on Saturday night, while at least three oil tankers were attacked near the Strait of Hormuz.
stories.stand: Bahrain said its air defences intercepted several attacks; neither Bahrain nor the US military confirmed Iran's claims of damage.
body: Iran fired two waves of drones and ballistic missiles at four US bases in Bahrain on Saturday night, according to Iranian media. Bahrain, which hosts the headquarters of the US Fifth Fleet, told residents to shelter.

Bahrain said its air defences intercepted several attacks and called them Iranian aggression. A civilian industrial compound caught fire, with no injuries reported. The Revolutionary Guards claimed to have hit two Patriot batteries and a radar, which Bahrain and the US military did not confirm.

At least three oil tankers were attacked near the Strait of Hormuz. The UK's maritime security agency, UKMTO, reported two struck by projectiles, with no casualties. More than 14 Iranian tankers were reported to be gathering off Kharg Island to challenge the US naval blockade.

Iran's foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, said reopening the strait would not be difficult if the US accepted Iran's conditions. President Donald Trump told Fox News he wants a permanent deal that stops Iran getting nuclear weapons.

stories.head: Iran claims it shot down two US drones as talks stay stalled
stories.say: Iran's Revolutionary Guards say they downed two American drones over the Strait of Hormuz on Saturday, and Tehran insists its seven conditions must be met to reopen the strait.
stories.stand: The US military did not comment on the claims; Iran's foreign minister also ruled out sending its enriched uranium abroad.
body: Iran's Revolutionary Guards said on Saturday that a new air defence system shot down a US MQ-9 drone over the Strait of Hormuz, according to state broadcaster IRIB. They later claimed an MQ-1 over Qeshm Island. The US military had no immediate comment.

On Friday, Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Iran's seven conditions must be met before the strait reopens. They include ending the war and lifting sanctions and the naval blockade of southern ports. He ruled out moving Iran's stockpile of uranium enriched to 60% abroad.
Also on Friday, the US Treasury sanctioned four Iranians it described as oil trustees. The US and Israel launched the war on 28 February.

stories.head: Russian strike on Zelenskyy's hometown kills two and wounds 60
stories.say: A Russian attack on Kryvyi Rih on Friday night killed a seven-year-old boy and a twenty-year-old woman and wounded sixty people, regional officials said.
stories.stand: About 25 apartment buildings, a hospital and schools were damaged in central Kryvyi Rih, the city's administration said.
body: A Russian strike on central Kryvyi Rih on Friday night killed two people, a 7-year-old boy and a 20-year-old woman, according to Oleksandr Hanzha, head of the regional military administration. He said 60 people were wounded, including six children.

Oleksandr Vilkul, head of the city administration, said the attack started four fires and damaged about 25 apartment buildings, a hospital, schools and an industrial site. Kryvyi Rih is President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's hometown.
A separate Russian drone attack on Kharkiv wounded 11 people, including two children, officials said.

stories.head: Eisenkot invites Netanyahu's Likud to Israeli coalition talks
stories.say: Gadi Eisenkot, who is trying to form Israel's next government, has invited Benjamin Netanyahu's Likud party to coalition talks, with a first meeting set for Sunday.
stories.stand: October's election left neither bloc with a clear majority; Eisenkot has until December to form a government and has ruled out serving under Netanyahu.
body: Gadi Eisenkot, the former military chief who leads the centrist Yashar party, invited Likud to coalition talks on Saturday, with the first meeting set for Sunday. Likud is led by caretaker Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
Eisenkot has until December to form a government after October's election gave neither bloc a clear majority. Yashar said the talks reflected a commitment to forming the broadest possible government.

Likud wants an end to personal attacks and a joint declaration excluding Arab parties. Former prime minister Naftali Bennett said his party would not join Netanyahu or his bloc. Eisenkot has ruled out serving under Netanyahu.

stories.stand: The 800-megawatt plant stopped running after the blaze; the cause has not been confirmed.

The Iraqi News Agency said civil defence teams brought the fire under control. Operations at the 800-megawatt plant stopped. The cause has not been confirmed.

stories.head: Toxic alcohol kills 11 and puts 180 in hospital in India's Manipur
stories.say: At least eleven people have died and more than a hundred and eighty have been taken to hospital after drinking suspected toxic alcohol in India's Manipur state.
stories.stand: Manipur's chief minister has ordered an investigation; officials urged anyone who drank alcohol from Sugnu town to get checked.
body: At least 11 people have died after drinking suspected spurious alcohol in Manipur, north-east India, Chief Minister Yumnam Khemchand Singh said on Friday. He said the deaths came in the previous 48 hours and ordered an inquiry.
More than 180 people had been admitted to hospitals as of Friday. Local media said officials advised anyone who had drunk alcohol from Sugnu town in the past week to seek medical checks.

stories.head: Three Americans convicted in Honduras over woman's 2022 disappearance
stories.say: A Honduran court has convicted four men, three of them US citizens, of criminal association over a woman who vanished while jet skiing near Roatán in 2022.
stories.stand: Two defendants were cleared of human trafficking for lack of evidence, and prosecutors say they will appeal and seek ten-year sentences.
body: A Honduran court on Friday convicted four people of criminal association over the disappearance of a woman near Roatán on 1 January 2022. Three of them are US citizens: Harold Green, William James Murdock and Gary Lee Johnston.

Green and Murdock were acquitted of human trafficking for insufficient evidence, and the Public Ministry said it would appeal. Prosecutors will seek the maximum 10-year sentence for each defendant. The next hearing is on 9 December.
The woman's whereabouts remain unknown. Her jet ski was found about 170 kilometres away in Belize.

stories.head: Bolsonaro in intensive care with intestinal blockage
stories.say: Brazil's former president Jair Bolsonaro has been admitted to intensive care in Brasília with an intestinal obstruction, his hospital says, though it describes him as stable.
stories.stand: Bolsonaro is serving a coup sentence under humanitarian house arrest; police escorted him to hospital after he fell ill at home.
body: Former Brazilian president Jair Bolsonaro was admitted to intensive care at the DF Star hospital in Brasília on Saturday with an intestinal obstruction. Military police escorted him from his home, where he is under house arrest.

The hospital said he was clinically stable, conscious and breathing without help. A gastric tube was inserted, and further surgery has not been ruled out. His son Carlos Bolsonaro raised the possibility of a tenth operation in under eight years.
Bolsonaro is serving a sentence of 27 years and three months for plotting a coup. Justice Alexandre de Moraes granted him humanitarian house arrest in March.

stories.head: Three French officers convicted of racist assault on music producer
stories.say: A Paris court has convicted three police officers of a racially motivated group assault on the music producer Michel Zecler, who was beaten outside his studio in 2020.
stories.stand: Each received five years, mostly suspended, and all are barred from the police; Zecler's lawyer said the sentences fell short.
body: The Paris criminal court on Friday convicted three police officers of aggravated, racially motivated group assault on Michel Zecler, a Black music producer. They were also convicted of falsifying a police report.
Officers stopped Zecler outside his Paris studio in November 2020 over a face-mask violation and beat him, delivering about 30 blows over around five minutes.
Each officer received five years, partly suspended, and all three are barred from rejoining the police. Zecler's lawyer said the sentences fell short.

stories.say: Francesco Schettino, captain of the Costa Concordia when it sank off Giglio in 2012, has been released on probation after more than nine years in a Rome prison.
stories.stand: The disaster killed 32 people; Schettino was sentenced to 16 years, and a Rome court approved his release after reviewing his conduct.
body: Francesco Schettino, former captain of the Costa Concordia, was released on probation from Rome's Rebibbia prison on Friday evening after more than nine years, according to the Italian outlet QN cited by Euronews.
The Rome Supervisory Court granted the release after reviewing his rehabilitation and conduct in prison.
The cruise ship struck rocks off Isola del Giglio in January 2012, and 32 people died. Schettino was sentenced to 16 years, upheld by Italy's highest court in 2017.

stories.head: Suffolk village votes 257 to 16 to 'leave UK' over asylum plan
stories.say: Barnham in Suffolk voted two hundred and fifty-seven to sixteen in a symbolic poll on Saturday to seek crown dependency status, protesting at plans to house asylum seekers nearby.
stories.stand: The vote has no legal weight; the government has not made a final decision on housing 931 men at the former RAF site.
body: Barnham, near Bury St Edmunds, held a symbolic referendum on Saturday on seeking crown dependency status, in protest at plans to house asylum seekers at RAF Barnham. The result was 257 votes for and 16 against, with one spoiled ballot. The vote has no legal weight.

The government first earmarked the site for up to 1,256 men, later cut to 931. Parish council chairman John Bauer said 400 to 500 people were eligible to vote. A similar poll was held in Piddington, Oxfordshire, in September.

Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch backed the residents. The Home Office said it was listening to concerns and was moving people out of hotels into former military sites with round-the-clock security. No final decision on RAF Barnham has been made.

stories.say: A man has been charged with attempted murder after the Bradford councillor Ibrar Ali was stabbed in the street on Thursday morning, West Yorkshire Police said.
stories.stand: The independent councillor remains in hospital in a serious but stable condition.
body: Ibrar Ali, 52, an independent councillor for Bradford Moor ward, was stabbed in Thornbury Avenue, Bradford, at around 11am on Thursday, West Yorkshire Police said. He remains in hospital in a serious but stable condition.

Police have charged Arfan Ali, 32, of Thornbury Avenue, with attempted murder, assault and possession of an offensive weapon in a public place. He was remanded in custody to appear at Leeds Magistrates' Court on Saturday. The charges are allegations and have not been tested in court.

stories.say: A kitchen porter at a Henley members' club has been jailed for life, with a minimum of twenty-two and a half years, for murdering a former Microsoft executive in the Thames.
stories.stand: Oxford Crown Court heard he hit her with a weight bar and held her underwater; he was already serving a suspended sentence for assault.
body: Nelio Gouveia, 45, was jailed for life with a minimum term of 22 years and six months at Oxford Crown Court, ITV News reported. He had admitted murdering a 44-year-old former Microsoft executive in Henley-on-Thames in March.

The court heard that Gouveia, a kitchen porter at the Phyllis Court members' club, struck her on the head with a metal weight-lifting bar and held her under the water for about 12 minutes. Drugs and alcohol were involved. He was serving a suspended sentence for an earlier assault at the time.
Mr Justice Jay described the killing as an exercise of power and a desire to dominate.

stories.say: A twenty-four-year-old man with extreme neo-Nazi views has been convicted of preparing a terrorist attack on a Hull hotel housing migrants, after a would-be accomplice went to police.
stories.stand: Officers found napalm, a Molotov cocktail, a crossbow and a machete; he will be sentenced next year.
body: Mikka Anderson, 24, was found guilty at Newcastle Crown Court of preparing an act of terrorism and possessing weapons for terrorist purposes, ITV News reported on Friday. He had denied both charges.

Prosecutors said he planned to firebomb the Royal Hotel in Hull, which houses migrants. He tried to recruit an accomplice, who went to police. Counter Terrorism Police said officers found body armour, homemade fuses, a crossbow, a machete, napalm and a ready-made Molotov cocktail.
Anderson said he was a survivalist who never meant to harm anyone. Mrs Justice Lambert will sentence him next year and said a very significant custodial sentence was very likely.

stories.head: Crane ready to lift collapsed Pero's Bridge from Bristol harbour
stories.say: A barge-mounted crane is in place to lift Bristol's Pero's Bridge out of the Floating Harbour, three weeks after it collapsed into the water.
stories.stand: The council hopes to reopen the footbridge in spring 2027; recovery will cost about £280,000.
body: A crane on a barge is ready to lift the three spans of Pero's Bridge out of Bristol's Floating Harbour and take them to Albion Dry Dock for inspection, ITV News reported on Saturday. The footbridge collapsed into the water at 11pm on 31 October. No one was injured.
Recovery will cost about £280,000, covered by an existing £1.51m refurbishment budget. The council hopes to reopen the bridge in spring 2027.

An engineering assessment suggests external vibration was the most likely contributing factor. A council report found the bridge had not been properly tested for almost a decade because of the weight of padlocks left on it.

stories.head: New £1.3bn rail line station sits unused over staffing dispute
stories.say: Winslow station in Buckinghamshire, built for the first stage of East West Rail, has stood unused for nearly two years because of a dispute over driver-only trains.
stories.stand: Chiltern Railways and the RMT union disagree over train manager roles; only freight and training trains have used the line.
body: Winslow station in Buckinghamshire was built nearly two years ago but has never opened to passengers, ITV News reported. It is on the first stage of East West Rail, from Oxford to Milton Keynes, which cost about £1.3bn.

Chiltern Railways and the RMT union are in dispute over driver-only operation, and only freight and driver training trains have run. RMT general secretary Eddie Dempsey said the union would keep campaigning for guarantees on train manager roles.
Chiltern's interim managing director, Tony Baxter, said the operator wanted to resolve the dispute. The Department for Transport said it backed efforts to start services as soon as possible.

stories.head: Police renew appeal two years after baby's remains found in Salford
stories.say: Greater Manchester Police are still appealing for information two years after the remains of a baby they call Ava were found in a field in Little Hulton, Salford.
stories.stand: A £50,000 reward is on offer, and detectives are still trying to trace the baby's mother.
body: Greater Manchester Police renewed their appeal on Friday, two years after the remains of a baby girl, named Ava by police, were found in Ashtons Field, Little Hulton, Salford, on 20 November 2024.
The baby was wrapped in women's underwear that detectives believe the mother may have worn while pregnant. The mother has not been traced. A £50,000 reward is on offer.
Detective Inspector Louise Kelly, the senior investigating officer, said police would not give up. Officers are working with the council to arrange a funeral.

stories.head: Miliband says 'all options' on EU ties are open, including rejoining
stories.say: Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband says all options for Britain's relationship with the European Union are on the table, including rejoining, after Andy Burnham signed three deals.
stories.stand: He said the new food, carbon and youth deals would apply whether or not a row over EU students' tuition fees is settled.
body: Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said rejoining the EU was open for discussion, telling the BBC that all the options would be on the table, ITV News reported on Saturday.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham plans a year of informal talks with Brussels while keeping Labour's 2024 red lines: no single market, no customs union and no freedom of movement.

On Friday Burnham signed deals on food checks, emissions trading and a youth scheme of up to 100,000 visas a year for 18 to 31-year-olds. EU states want their students to pay domestic tuition fees. Miliband said the deals would apply regardless of that dispute.

stories.head: SNP would back Burnham as prime minister in a hung parliament
stories.say: The SNP's leadership has decided its MPs would back Andy Burnham as prime minister in a hung parliament without upfront demands, ITV News reports.
stories.stand: Senior SNP figures would instead press for a second independence referendum through budget and confidence votes.
body: The SNP leadership has decided that its MPs would support Labour leader Andy Burnham as prime minister if the next general election produced a hung parliament, with no upfront demands, ITV News Border reported on Saturday.

Senior SNP figures plan to press their demands, including a second independence referendum, through confidence and supply votes such as budgets. Burnham has said Scottish independence is off the table and told ITV there will be no general election in 2027.

stories.head: SNP cancels £60,000 loan owed to jailed ex-chief executive Peter Murrell
stories.say: The SNP's ruling body has cancelled a sixty thousand pound debt owed to Peter Murrell, the former chief executive jailed for embezzling more than four hundred thousand pounds from the party.
stories.stand: A court hearing on 7 December will decide how much Murrell must pay back under proceeds of crime law.
body: The SNP's National Executive Committee agreed on Saturday to cancel a £60,000 loan the party owed to its former chief executive, Peter Murrell, ITV News reported. The party said the loan had been cancelled and removed from its accounts.

Murrell, the estranged husband of former first minister Nicola Sturgeon, admitted in May to embezzling more than £400,000 from the party and was jailed for more than five years. He lent the party the money in 2021.
A Proceeds of Crime Act hearing on 7 December will decide how much will be confiscated. The same meeting replaced Angela Constance with Shona Robison as the party's business convener.

stories.say: Wales's First Minister Rhun ap Iorwerth has accused Andy Burnham of turning his back on Wales after the prime minister refused to devolve policing, justice, rail and the Crown Estate.
stories.stand: Burnham wrote that he was not persuaded on policing, citing the joint England and Wales system.
body: Prime Minister Andy Burnham has ruled out transferring more powers to the Welsh government, including policing and justice, the Crown Estate and rail infrastructure, ITV News Wales reported on Saturday.

First Minister Rhun ap Iorwerth said Burnham showed more respect to English regions than to Wales, and that he had more say over policing as mayor of Greater Manchester than ap Iorwerth has as first minister.

In a letter, Burnham said he was not persuaded on devolving policing, citing the integrated England and Wales system. Welsh Secretary Stephen Kinnock said the prime minister had offered a partnership on growth and jobs.

stories.stand: He called the Russian missiles and drone that fell in Poland an outrageous provocation and said allies must do more for Ukraine.

stories.stand: Three newcomers back Van Hollen and one backs Schumer, with the rest undecided or uncommitted, according to AP.
body: Democrats will choose their Senate majority leader in a secret ballot on 1 December, with longtime leader Chuck Schumer of New York challenged by Chris Van Hollen of Maryland, AP reported.

The 13 incoming Democratic senators are the largest new class in decades. Abdul El-Sayed, Peggy Flanagan and Elissa Slotkin back Van Hollen. Sherrod Brown backs Schumer. Several, including Mary Peltola and James Talarico, are undecided.
Jon Ossoff said he had not committed to any candidate. The groups MoveOn and Indivisible have endorsed Van Hollen.

stories.head: Trump orders federal contractors to consult White House on Congress inquiries
stories.say: Donald Trump has ordered federal contractors to coordinate with the White House before answering congressional inquiries, or risk losing their contracts.
stories.stand: Democrats called the order an attack on Congress's oversight powers; the White House says it protects executive privilege.
body: President Donald Trump issued an executive order late on Friday requiring federal contractors and subcontractors to consult the White House on congressional inquiries, AP reported. Companies must withhold communications the White House considers privileged.
Firms that do not comply could have contracts terminated and be suspended from future federal work. The order covers tens of thousands of businesses.

Representative Robert Garcia, the top Democrat on the House Oversight Committee, called it a blatant attack on Congress's right to conduct oversight. Representative Jamie Raskin called it unlawful. The White House said it was protecting executive privileges from overreach.

stories.head: Voters oust some US sheriffs whose deputies worked with ICE
stories.say: Several US sheriffs who signed up to help immigration enforcement lost their seats in November, AP reports, including in North Carolina, Maryland and Wisconsin.
stories.stand: Agreements letting local officers act for ICE have grown to more than 2,700, from 135.
body: Some sheriffs who backed President Donald Trump's immigration enforcement lost their re-election races, AP reported after reviewing about 250 sheriff contests.

In Alamance County, North Carolina, independent Shannon Long beat Republican Sheriff Terry Johnson and says he will not join the 287(g) programme. In Frederick County, Maryland, Democrat Karl Bickel defeated Republican Sheriff Chuck Jenkins, who said the programme likely cost him.
The 287(g) agreements let local officers carry out some immigration enforcement. They now number more than 2,700, up from 135, and have deputised more than 29,000 local officers.

stories.stand: The Financial Supervisory Commission also raised the margin for short-selling; it is the first blanket curb of its kind since 2015.
body: Taiwan's Financial Supervisory Commission said on Saturday it would ban short-selling of stocks that fell in the previous session from Monday 23 November, Focus Taiwan reported. It is the first blanket curb of its kind since 2015. The minimum margin for short-selling rises from 130% to 150%.

The TAIEX fell 2,393.60 points, or 6.23%, to 36,033.29 on Friday, its lowest close in nearly seven months. Its intraday low was more than 28% below the record high of 6 October. The fall followed heavy losses in AI-related stocks worldwide.

stories.head: EU and Indonesia sign trade deal after a decade of talks
stories.say: The EU and Indonesia have signed a trade deal that removes ninety-eight and a half per cent of tariffs on EU goods, saving exporters more than six hundred million euros a year.
stories.stand: The European Commission expects EU exports to Indonesia to rise by nearly 40% within 15 years; ratification is still needed.
body: The European Union and Indonesia signed trade and investment agreements on Saturday, ending about a decade of negotiations, Euronews reported. Commission President Ursula von der Leyen called it a momentous day.
The deal will lift 98.5% of tariffs on EU goods, saving EU exporters more than €600 million a year. Trade between them was worth €28.9 billion in 2025.
The Commission expects EU exports to Indonesia to rise by nearly 40% within 15 years. The European Parliament and Indonesia must ratify it, and it could apply from early next year.

stories.head: Africa's new credit rating agency plans first ratings by March
stories.say: The African Union's new credit rating agency, based in Mauritius, expects to publish its first ratings of governments by the end of March and is in talks with fifteen countries.
stories.stand: Its interim chief says the aim is not to manufacture better ratings for Africa; Moody's says African default risk matches other regions.
body: The Africa Credit Rating Agency, launched by the African Union on 7 October, expects its first sovereign ratings by the end of March, Al Jazeera reported. It is based in Port Louis, Mauritius, and is in talks with 15 governments.

Interim chief executive Sifiso Falala said the objective was not to manufacture better ratings for Africa. The agency is privately owned and governments will pay for their ratings. It also plans to rate cities, banks and local-currency debt.
A 2023 UNDP study estimated that subjective ratings cost African countries $74.5bn. Moody's says a B-rated African country has about a 5% chance of default in a year, the same as elsewhere.

stories.head: Two rival claims to have proved the Riemann hypothesis
stories.say: An Anthropic mathematician says he and Claude have proved the generalised Riemann hypothesis, while a Stanford researcher has presented a separate, entirely human proof.
stories.stand: The AI-assisted proof compiles in the Lean checking language, but no human has yet read and understood the full argument.
body: Levent Alpöge, a mathematician at Anthropic, has posted a proof of the generalised Riemann hypothesis written in Lean, a programming language that checks proofs, TechCrunch and Al Jazeera reported. He said he worked through the argument with Claude, which he said far outpaced him near the finish.

Several mathematicians, including MIT's Andrew Sutherland, report that the Lean code compiles. But human mathematicians still need to read and understand it. Kevin Buzzard of Imperial College London expects that within weeks.

Separately, Stanford postdoc Alessandro Masullo presented a human proof based on 12 years of work, posted by Ravi Vakil, president of the American Mathematical Society. It has not been checked in Lean. The problem is one of the Clay Millennium Prize Problems, which carry $1m.

stories.head: Himalaya-sized ancient mountains found hidden beneath Antarctica
stories.say: Researchers have found the roots of ancient mountain ranges as big as the Himalayas beneath Antarctica's ice, formed more than four hundred and fifty million years ago.
stories.stand: The team dated 1,712 zircon grains from ocean sediments; erosion of the peaks may have helped set up the Cambrian explosion of life.
body: Scientists from the Australian National University and Germany's GFZ research centre have identified the roots of previously unknown mountain ranges beneath Antarctica, similar in scale to the Himalayas, Euronews reported. The study is in Earth and Planetary Science Letters.
The mountains formed 650 to 450 million years ago as the Gondwana supercontinent came together. The team dated 1,712 zircon grains from sediments drilled along the continent's edge.
The researchers suggest rapid erosion of the mountains fed nutrients into the oceans and raised oxygen levels, which may have helped set the stage for the Cambrian explosion.

stories.stand: The University of São Paulo study of 38 cats suggests they aim their calls at people, though whether it is deliberate is unclear.
body: Researchers at the University of São Paulo watched 38 pet cats in front of a closed box holding their favourite food, which they could smell but not open, Euronews reported.

The researchers say this suggests cats direct their calls at people who might help, but it is unclear whether it is a conscious strategy.

stories.stand: The merger, nicknamed Bao, took about seven orbits; the study is published in Nature.
body: A smaller star spiralled into a supergiant in the Andromeda galaxy and merged with it, astronomers led by Columbia University's Viraj Karambelkar report in Nature, ScienceDaily said. They say it is the first such event identified.
The giant was about 7 times the Sun's mass and its companion about 0.7. The merger took about seven orbits. The eruption, catalogued as AT 2025abao and nicknamed Bao, was detected on 17 October 2025.
The team combined mid-infrared observations from the James Webb Space Telescope with data from several other observatories and computer simulations.

stories.stand: The team says a new motion-control method could boost sensitivity 100 to 1,000 times; the work is still theoretical.
body: A team led by Kyushu University, with NIST, the University of Waterloo and others, proposes that a clock could tick at a superposition of different rates, ScienceDaily reported. The effect has never been observed. The paper is in Physical Review Letters.

They suggest testing it with trapped-ion atomic clocks, where the clock's motion would become entangled with its internal energy. A new motion-control method could raise sensitivity 100 to 1,000 times.
The work is theoretical. Designing a detailed experiment is the next step.

body: Federal and local authorities dismantled what they describe as the first nitazene synthesis lab in the US, in the basement of a home in Baton Rouge, Louisiana, CBS News reported. Investigators had thought it was making fentanyl.

body: A jury at Gloucestershire Coroner's Court found on Friday that the death of a 33-year-old mother of five after a liquid buttock-lift procedure in Gloucester in September 2024 was accidental, ITV News reported. Her family said they were very disappointed.
Hyaluronic acid filler moved through her blood into her brain, lungs and heart. The procedure was carried out in an at-home beauty room. The practitioner died in February 2026 and was never charged.
The coroner will issue a prevention of future deaths report. A government consultation on restricting such procedures runs until January 2027.

body: COP31 talks in Antalya, Turkey, ran past their Friday deadline. Summit president Murat Kurum said a revised text had been put forward that all parties could agree, with approval scheduled for Sunday, Reuters reported via The Spokesman-Review.

Some decisions were adopted earlier, including on cooperation under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement. The next summit will be in Addis Ababa in November 2027.
